messages.subject: Options to manage Java Heap Space error, or Out of space to write reduced objects error when handling large data.
messages.subject_clean: Options to manage Java Heap Space error, or Out of space to write reduced objects error when handling large data.
messages.body_plain:
I am working  on a 5TB dataset that has a considerable number of keys. And the number of values are a bit skewed. Most of them have reasonable number of values while some have really big number of values. These values are being structured as a dataframe for each key.
Now this is where the problem is. While this data is being emitted, collected and collated there are some nodes which completely run out of space even if, finally they have enough space to store the reduced data.

As the data is extremely large I avoided using post in my reduce code as I was pretty sure that I would run out of memory. So I just use reduce-> reduce making it easy for the reduce to quickly write data back to hdfs as they come. But now I ran out of disk space to write the reduced object. So to fix this issue I use the combiner option. My understanding was the combiner would reduce the memory usage by locally reducing the keys, reducing the keys first and the collating them. But I seem to have run out of memory when using combiner too. Now the only option I can think of is to play with mapred.reduce.slowstart.completed.maps. I am varying it between 0.4 to 0.9 to see how the memory usage is, and without a combiner. I have two questions,

1. Is there any other solution that I can use to optimize large data other than what I am doing?
2. Is it possible that I write the keys immediately to HDFS and then retrieve then when being reduced? I know this will increase time but might atleast prevent failed jobs. One way of doing this might be first to just map the data and write them to HDFS. And then reduce them, but I am not very sure how efficient that would be.

Thanks,
Ashrith

messages.body_plain:
I would be suspicious of your code in general (or those pesky Java settings looking at you multithreaded garbage collection).

You said you could do your work in reduce/reduce which implies two things:
1) You don't need to see all the reduce key data before creating your new reduced data.
2) For the parts you do they must be rather small almost insignificant.

In general if your reduce isn't behaving well your keyspace is badly designed.  It seems like you have little care about what gets reduced together, so why not just add something to the key to break apart those big reduces when you emit in the Map? (Suggestion 1)  If anything you since you said you can use a collect, you can use this new keyspace for one MapReduce job and then fix it back up in a second.  To pull this off you usually need a MapReduce to present a little metadata on your keyspace.

Barring that and the reduce data does have to stay together.  Why not pick it apart more in the map and emit less stuff out of it? (Suggestion 2)

Barring those two being possible is usually that means you are trying to reduce based on the distribution of values you have encountered in a reduce?  (See now I am just speculating)  In which case you need to get a little creative with perhaps picking out a few variables as their own part of the key, and then do it in two MapReduces, which is suggestion 1 in disguise.   For example this can be done, Map newkey = ( old key, var 1),  Map: newkey (old key, var 2).  The reduce works over the variables separately for your keys, and then you make a new MapReduce to drop the var from the key and reassemble the data.frame.

Its really hard to answer these questions without knowing what sort of reduce you are trying to pull off =)

Good luck,
Jeremiah
